instruction: WRITE AN AUTOLISP ROUTING FOR AUTOCAD TO DELETE THE ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP DICTIONARY ENTITY
output:
Below is one example of an AutoLISP routine that uses ActiveX methods to open the Named Objects Dictionary, check for the existence of the dictionary named "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP" and, if found, remove it. (Always save your drawing and back up any custom data before running routines that delete database objects.) 

To use the routine:
1. Copy and paste the code into a text editor and save it with an .lsp extension.
2. Load the LISP file into AutoCAD with APPLOAD.
3. Run the command (for example, DELDGNLSTYLE) to delete the dictionary.

------------------------------------------------------------
(defun c:DELGNDGNLINESTYLECOMP ( / acadApp doc nod dgnObj result)
  (vl-load-com)  ; Ensure that VLISP functions are available
  ;; Get the AutoCAD application and active document objects
  (setq acadApp (vlax-get-acad-object))
  (setq doc (vla-get-ActiveDocument acadApp))
  ;; Get the Named Objects Dictionary
  (setq nod (vla-get-NamedObjectsDictionary doc))
  ;; Try to retrieve the dictionary "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP"
  (setq dgnObj (vl-catch-all-apply 'vlax-get-property (list nod 'Item "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP")))
  (if (vl-catch-all-error-p dgnObj)
    (progn
      (princ "\nThe ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP dictionary does not exist in this drawing.")
    )
    (progn
      ;; Remove the dictionary from the Named Objects Dictionary.
      ;; (vlax-invoke nod 'Remove "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP") deletes the item.
      (vl-catch-all-apply 'vlax-invoke-method (list nod 'Remove "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP"))
      (princ "\nThe ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP dictionary was successfully deleted.")
    )
  )
  (princ)
)
------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation of key parts:
• (vl-load-com) – loads the Visual LISP COM interface.
• (vlax-get-acad-object) and (vla-get-ActiveDocument …) – obtain handles to the AutoCAD application and the current drawing.
• (vla-get-NamedObjectsDictionary doc) – accesses the Named Objects Dictionary where custom dictionaries (like ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP) are stored.
• (vlax-get-property (list nod 'Item "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP")) – attempts to get the dictionary. If it doesn’t exist an error is caught.
• (vlax-invoke-method nod 'Remove "ACAD_DGNLINESTYLECOMP") – deletes the item from the dictionary.

Always test such routines on sample drawings before applying them to critical work files.

instruction: How can I restrict a Postgres geometry column to only contain polygons?
I'm trying to run a pytorch program on a computer with multiple GPUs. My program is only using one! What can I change in the code to get it to use all the gpus available?
output:
There are a couple of common approaches in PyTorch to utilize multiple GPUs:

1. Use nn.DataParallel:
 • Wrap your model with torch.nn.DataParallel. For example, if your code currently creates the model like this:

  model = MyModel()

 then modify it as follows:

  if torch.cuda.device_count() > 1:
   print("Let's use", torch.cuda.device_count(), "GPUs!")
   model = torch.nn.DataParallel(model)

 Finally, move your model to the appropriate GPU (often cuda:0):
  model = model.to("cuda:0")

 DataParallel automatically splits your batch across the available GPUs and gathers the results.

2. Use DistributedDataParallel:
 • For even better performance when scaling, you might consider torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel (DDP). This requires you to launch multiple processes (one per GPU) and perform some extra setup for initializing the process group. The basic structure looks like:

  import torch.distributed as dist
  import torch.multiprocessing as mp

  def main_worker(gpu, ngpus, ...):
   torch.cuda.set_device(gpu)
   dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl", init_method="env://", world_size=ngpus, rank=gpu)
   model = MyModel().to(gpu)
   model = torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel(model, device_ids=[gpu])
   # rest of training loop...

  if __name__ == '__main__':
   ngpus = torch.cuda.device_count()
   mp.spawn(main_worker, nprocs=ngpus, args=(ngpus,...))

Choose DataParallel for minimal code changes and if your batch sizes are large enough to be split among GPUs, or DDP if you need more scalability and efficiency.

Also, double-check:
 • That your environment variable CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES isn’t restricting GPU usage.
 • That your input data batching is set up properly.

By applying one of these changes, your program should be able to utilize all your available GPUs.

instruction: I have a system76 Thelio linux computer. I would like to install a Nvidia GTX 3060 GPU. I have a 450W PSU. First, is the psu sufficient to power the gpu? Second, how do I install the gpu?
output:
Below are answers to your two questions regarding a System76 Thelio running Linux, a GTX 3060 installation, and your 450W PSU:

─────────────────────────────  
1. PSU Suitability

• Power Draw and Recommendations  
 – The GTX 3060’s typical board power is around 170 watts.  
 – However, NVIDIA and many board partners usually recommend a PSU rated around 550 watts for a complete system using a 3060. This recommendation accounts for headroom, possible load spikes from the CPU and other components, and overall system stability.

• Your 450W PSU in Context  
 – If your system has been designed with low-power parts and light overclocking, the 450W PSU might closely cover your needs under nominal conditions.  
 – That said, installing a GTX 3060 pushes the overall system power demands near the lower limit. Unexpected load spikes or future upgrades could lead to instability or shutdowns.  
 – In many cases, users upgrading to a 3060 also upgrade their PSU to ensure proper headroom for safety and longevity.  

So, while your 450W PSU may “run” the GPU in certain configurations, it isn’t an ideal match. You may want to consider upgrading to a higher-wattage, high-quality PSU (around 550–650W) to be safe.

─────────────────────────────  
2. Installing the GPU

Assuming you decide to proceed or have upgraded your PSU, here are the general steps to install a PCI Express (PCIe) GPU into your Linux system:

A. Preparation  
 1. Power Off and Unplug:  
  – Shut down your computer completely and disconnect it from mains power.  
  – Press the power button briefly (if needed) to fully discharge capacitors.  

 2. Ground Yourself:  
  – Use an anti-static wrist strap or periodically touch a grounded metal surface to avoid static discharge damaging components.

 3. Gather Tools:  
  – Typically, you’ll need a Phillips-head screwdriver and possibly a pair of tweezers or cable ties for cable management.

B. Physical Installation  
 1. Open the Case:  
  – Remove the case cover per your system’s manual. The Thelio’s design might have specific instructions—check System76’s documentation if available.

 2. Locate the PCIe x16 Slot:  
  – Find the primary PCIe x16 slot on your motherboard.  
  – Remove the corresponding expansion slot bracket(s) from the back of the case where the GPU’s outputs will reside.

 3. Insert the GPU:  
  – Carefully align the GPU with the PCIe slot.  
  – Firmly seat the GPU into the slot until the card’s retention clip (if present) clicks into place.  
  – Ensure that the GPU’s display ports align with the rear I/O opening.

 4. Connect Power Cables:  
  – Many GTX 3060 cards require an additional PCIe power connector (often an 8-pin or 6+2-pin cable).  
  – Check your card’s requirements and connect the appropriate cables from the PSU to the GPU. Make sure that the cable is firmly seated.

 5. Secure the Card:  
  – Use the screws provided to fasten the GPU bracket to the case. This helps keep the card properly seated.

C. Post-Installation  
 1. Reassemble:  
  – Replace the case cover and reattach any cables you previously removed.

 2. Power On:  
  – Plug your system in and turn it on.  
  – Enter the BIOS/UEFI if you need to confirm that the GPU is detected.

D. Installing NVIDIA Drivers on Linux  
 1. Update System Packages:  
  – Open a terminal and update your repositories (commands depend on your distro, e.g., “sudo apt update” for Ubuntu-based systems).

 2. Install Proprietary Drivers:  
  – Many Linux distributions now offer an “Additional Drivers” tool (such as Ubuntu’s “Software & Updates”) which will detect and install the recommended NVIDIA driver.  
  – Alternatively, you can install drivers via the terminal by installing packages like “nvidia-driver-XXX” (replace “XXX” with the driver version recommended for your 3060). Check System76 or your distro’s documentation for any quirks.

 3. Reboot:  
  – After installation of NVIDIA drivers, reboot your system.  
  – Confirm that the GPU is active (using commands such as “nvidia-smi” or checking settings in your Linux distribution’s GPU management tools).

─────────────────────────────  
Additional Considerations

• Warranty and Support:  
 – Modifying your System76 Thelio (especially regarding PSU changes) might affect your warranty or support status. It’s a good idea to review System76’s guidelines or contact their support if you’re unsure.

• Compatibility and Case Clearance:  
 – Verify that the physical dimensions of your chosen GTX 3060 card will fit within your Thelio case. This includes length, height, and any potential interference with other components.

• Backup:  
 – Before making hardware changes, it’s wise to back up any critical data.

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion

• PSU: The 450W PSU is on the low side for a system with a GTX 3060; while it might work under limited load, for better stability and safe headroom, a PSU upgrade to around 550–650W is advisable.  
• GPU Installation: Physically installing the GPU involves powering off the system, opening the case, seating the card into a PCIe slot, connecting the proper power cables, securing the card, and then installing appropriate NVIDIA drivers in Linux.

By taking these careful steps, you can successfully add a GTX 3060 to your System76 Thelio system while ensuring system stability.

instruction: write the gdscript code for a voxxel terrain engiune like minecraft in godot engine
output:
Below is one example of how you might begin building a basic voxel‐terrain (a “chunk” of cubes) engine in Godot using GDScript. This sample creates a single chunk (for example, 16×16×16 blocks) and generates its mesh using a SurfaceTool. (Note that a production‐ready Minecraft‐like engine would be far more complex, with many optimizations, multithreading, level‐of‐detail and neighbor–chunk handling, but this example shows the basic idea.) 

1. Create a new scene with a MeshInstance3D node (or in Godot 3.x a MeshInstance) and attach the following script (for Godot 4 use MeshInstance3D; adjust naming if needed):

────────────────────
# VoxelChunk.gd
extends MeshInstance3D

# Set the chunk dimensions; you might later want to make these configurable.
const CHUNK_SIZE = 16
# A 3D array to hold voxel data
var voxel_data = []

# Called when the node is added to the scene.
func _ready() -> void:
	# Create a flat terrain: fill lower layers with a solid value (1) and air (0) above.
	voxel_data = []
	for x in range(CHUNK_SIZE):
		voxel_data.append([])
		for y in range(CHUNK_SIZE):
			voxel_data[x].append([])
			for z in range(CHUNK_SIZE):
				# Example: simple “height” where half of the chunk is ground.
				var ground_height = CHUNK_SIZE / 2
				if y < ground_height:
					voxel_data[x][y].append(1)  # block type 1 (solid)
				else:
					voxel_data[x][y].append(0)  # air
	# Generate the mesh from the voxel data.
	generate_mesh()


# Generates the mesh by looping over the voxels and adding cube faces when a neighboring voxel is air.
func generate_mesh() -> void:
	var st = SurfaceTool.new()
	st.begin(Mesh.PRIMITIVE_TRIANGLES)
	var vertex_count = 0
	
	for x in range(CHUNK_SIZE):
		for y in range(CHUNK_SIZE):
			for z in range(CHUNK_SIZE):
				# Only add geometry if this voxel isn’t air.
				if voxel_data[x][y][z] != 0:
					var pos = Vector3(x, y, z)
					# For each of the six faces check if the neighboring voxel is air
					if is_air(x - 1, y, z): 
						vertex_count = add_face(st, pos, Vector3(-1, 0, 0), vertex_count)
					if is_air(x + 1, y, z):
						vertex_count = add_face(st, pos, Vector3(1, 0, 0), vertex_count)
					if is_air(x, y - 1, z):
						vertex_count = add_face(st, pos, Vector3(0, -1, 0), vertex_count)
					if is_air(x, y + 1, z):
						vertex_count = add_face(st, pos, Vector3(0, 1, 0), vertex_count)
					if is_air(x, y, z - 1):
						vertex_count = add_face(st, pos, Vector3(0, 0, -1), vertex_count)
					if is_air(x, y, z + 1):
						vertex_count = add_face(st, pos, Vector3(0, 0, 1), vertex_count)
	
	st.index() # build indices if needed
	var mesh = st.commit()
	# Assign the mesh to this MeshInstance3D so it is rendered.
	self.mesh = mesh


# Returns true if the given coordinates are out-of-bounds (and are then assumed to be air)
# or if the voxel is air.
func is_air(x: int, y: int, z: int) -> bool:
	if x < 0 or x >= CHUNK_SIZE or y < 0 or y >= CHUNK_SIZE or z < 0 or z >= CHUNK_SIZE:
		return true
	return voxel_data[x][y][z] == 0


# Adds a face (a quad made up of two triangles) to the SurfaceTool.
# normal: the face’s normal (which determines its orientation)
# pos: the position of the current voxel
# vertex_count: the number of vertices already added (used for indexing)
#
# Returns the updated vertex count.
func add_face(st: SurfaceTool, pos: Vector3, normal: Vector3, vertex_count: int) -> int:
	# Determine the four corner offsets based on the face normal.
	# The cube is 1×1×1; each face is a quad.
	var face_vertices = []

	if normal == Vector3(0, 0, 1):  # front face
		face_vertices = [
			Vector3(0, 0, 1),
			Vector3(1, 0, 1),
			Vector3(1, 1, 1),
			Vector3(0, 1, 1)
		]
	elif normal == Vector3(0, 0, -1):  # back face
		face_vertices = [
			Vector3(1, 0, 0),
			Vector3(0, 0, 0),
			Vector3(0, 1, 0),
			Vector3(1, 1, 0)
		]
	elif normal == Vector3(1, 0, 0):  # right face
		face_vertices = [
			Vector3(1, 0, 1),
			Vector3(1, 0, 0),
			Vector3(1, 1, 0),
			Vector3(1, 1, 1)
		]
	elif normal == Vector3(-1, 0, 0):  # left face
		face_vertices = [
			Vector3(0, 0, 0),
			Vector3(0, 0, 1),
			Vector3(0, 1, 1),
			Vector3(0, 1, 0)
		]
	elif normal == Vector3(0, 1, 0):  # top face
		face_vertices = [
			Vector3(0, 1, 1),
			Vector3(1, 1, 1),
			Vector3(1, 1, 0),
			Vector3(0, 1, 0)
		]
	elif normal == Vector3(0, -1, 0):  # bottom face
		face_vertices = [
			Vector3(0, 0, 0),
			Vector3(1, 0, 0),
			Vector3(1, 0, 1),
			Vector3(0, 0, 1)
		]
	
	# Add the vertices and the corresponding normals.
	for v in face_vertices:
		st.add_normal(normal)
		st.add_vertex(pos + v)
	
	# Create two triangles for the quad (with counter-clockwise winding).
	st.add_index(vertex_count + 0)
	st.add_index(vertex_count + 1)
	st.add_index(vertex_count + 2)
	st.add_index(vertex_count + 2)
	st.add_index(vertex_count + 3)
	st.add_index(vertex_count + 0)
	
	return vertex_count + 4
────────────────────

Explanation of the code:

• The _ready() function sets up a 3D array (voxel_data) with dimensions CHUNK_SIZE × CHUNK_SIZE × CHUNK_SIZE and fills it with a simple “flat world” (solid blocks below a given height).

• generate_mesh() loops over each voxel and checks each of its six faces. If a neighboring voxel is “air” (or the coordinate is outside the chunk), that face is added to the mesh.

• is_air() returns true when a coordinate is either outside the chunk or contains a 0 (designated as air).

• add_face() uses a Face’s normal to decide which four vertices (relative offsets within the unit cube) to add. It adds these vertices (and their normals) to the SurfaceTool and then defines two triangles using indices. A vertex_count variable is maintained so that indices can be defined correctly as vertices accumulate.

This basic example is only a starting point. A full “Minecraft‐like” voxel engine would include features such as:

• Using noise functions (e.g. OpenSimplexNoise) to create varied terrain.  
• Splitting the world into multiple chunks with neighbor–chunk communication to avoid “seams.”  
• Optimizing the mesh (merging faces, using greedy meshing, etc.).  
• Handling different block types/texturing via atlases and shaders.  
• Efficiently updating the mesh when blocks change.  

However, this script gives you a foundation to explore and expand your voxel terrain engine using Godot and GDScript. Enjoy building!

instruction: what are some good popular engines to develop web build games? list pros and cons of each, bonus points if it is unlikely to be outdated soon
output:
Below are some popular engines and frameworks for developing games that run in web browsers. Many of these are actively maintained and built on modern web standards, making them unlikely to be outdated soon. Here’s an overview with their pros and cons:

──────────────────────────────
1. Unity (with WebGL export)
──────────────────────────────
Pros:
• Mature Ecosystem: Unity has been around a long time with extensive documentation, tutorials, and a vast asset store.
• Cross‐Platform: Aside from WebGL builds, it can target almost any platform, letting you reuse much of your code.
• Powerful 2D and 3D Capabilities: Suitable for both simple and complex game designs.
• Community & Support: A huge global community ensures lots of forums, add-ons, and third‐party tools.

Cons:
• Build Size & Performance: WebGL builds may be large and require modern hardware; optimizing for lower-end devices might be challenging.
• Licensing: While the free tier is quite generous, revenue thresholds or advanced features might require subscription packages.
• Complexity: For simple or small-scale projects, Unity’s robust features can feel overwhelming.

──────────────────────────────
2. Godot Engine
──────────────────────────────
Pros:
• Open Source & Free: No licensing fees and complete access to modify the engine.
• Lightweight & Fast: Known for a smaller footprint, it often performs well even in less demanding environments.
• Dual 2D/3D Engine: Godot boasts separate, specialized pipelines for 2D and 3D, which can improve performance.
• Active Development: Constant improvements and growing community mean web exports are continually refined.

Cons:
• HTML5 Export Maturity: Although improving, the HTML5 export may sometimes face performance or compatibility issues compared to desktop builds.
• Smaller Community: While growing, it is still more niche than Unity’s community, meaning fewer ready-made assets or tutorials in some cases.
• Fewer Features: Some high-end features might still be under development or less polished than in more commercial engines.

──────────────────────────────
3. Phaser
──────────────────────────────
Pros:
• Pure HTML5 & JavaScript: Designed from the ground up for web games, making integration with web APIs simple.
• Lightweight & Fast: Particularly great for 2D games with excellent performance in the browser.
• Open Source: Fully MIT-licensed, with a simple, code-first approach that lets you understand every part of your game.
• Extensive Examples: A rich set of demos and tutorials makes it easy to learn.

Cons:
• 2D Focused: Not suited for sophisticated 3D games.
• Code-Centric: Lacks a visual editor, which means more manual coding compared to some “drag-and-drop” systems.
• Ecosystem Size: While robust for 2D, it might require combining with other tools (e.g., physics libraries) for more advanced needs.

──────────────────────────────
4. PlayCanvas
──────────────────────────────
Pros:
• Web-Native: Entirely built for browser-based games with a fully online development environment.
• Real-Time Collaboration: The cloud-based editor allows multiple developers to work on the project simultaneously.
• Lightweight & Fast: Optimized for modern browsers and devices.
• Intuitive: A good balance between visual editing and code freedom.

Cons:
• Ecosystem & Community: Smaller than Unity or Godot, which can mean fewer tutorials or third-party plugins.
• Offline Limitations: Being cloud-based may be a drawback if you prefer or require offline development.
• Feature Depth: May lack some of the deep, enterprise-level features that are available in larger engines.

──────────────────────────────
5. Three.js
──────────────────────────────
Pros:
• Focused 3D Library: Ideal for 3D games or interactive web experiences with robust rendering capabilities.
• Lightweight & Flexible: Provides low-level access so you can build custom game engines or visualization tools as needed.
• Actively Maintained: A huge community of developers continuously improves and expands its capabilities.
• Native Web Integration: Works seamlessly with other web technologies and standards.

Cons:
• Not a “Full” Engine: It’s primarily a rendering library, meaning you’ll need to integrate additional libraries or develop your own systems for physics, audio, or scene management.
• Steeper Learning Curve for Complex Projects: Building a complete game system from scratch can be time-consuming.
• More Boilerplate: More work is required to set up the game architecture compared to higher-level engines.

──────────────────────────────
Bonus Considerations for Longevity:
• All the engines listed here are built on technologies (like WebGL, HTML5, and JavaScript) that have strong industry backing; this means they’re likely to be supported and updated for the foreseeable future.
• Open source engines like Godot and Phaser benefit from community contributions, which helps keep them up-to-date.
• Unity and Three.js, due to their widespread adoption and continuous enterprise investment, are also likely to remain relevant for web game development.

Your choice will ultimately depend on your project’s complexity, your programming preferences, and the balance you’re seeking between ease of use and control. Happy developing!

instruction: Write edge test cases for the following condition: FICO > 750 && FICO <= 900 AND N_INQ < 2
output:
Below is a list of edge test cases for the compound condition:

  (FICO > 750 && FICO <= 900) AND (N_INQ < 2)

Remember that both parts must be satisfied for the overall condition to pass.

──────────────────────────────
1. Test Case: Minimum Valid FICO with Valid N_INQ
  • FICO = 751     // Just above 750 (the lower boundary)
  • N_INQ = 1     // Within boundary since 1 < 2
  Expected Result: PASS

──────────────────────────────
2. Test Case: Valid FICO with N_INQ at the Boundary
  • FICO = 751     // Valid (751 > 750)
  • N_INQ = 2     // Exactly 2, which does not satisfy “< 2”
  Expected Result: FAIL

──────────────────────────────
3. Test Case: FICO Exactly on the Lower Unaccepted Boundary
  • FICO = 750     // Fails the FICO > 750 check
  • N_INQ = 1     // Even though N_INQ is valid, FICO fails
  Expected Result: FAIL

──────────────────────────────
4. Test Case: Maximum Valid FICO with Valid N_INQ
  • FICO = 900     // Meets FICO <= 900 
  • N_INQ = 1     // Within boundary since 1 < 2
  Expected Result: PASS

──────────────────────────────
5. Test Case: FICO Above Maximum
  • FICO = 901     // Exceeds the maximum allowed (should be <= 900)
  • N_INQ = 1     // Valid N_INQ but FICO condition fails
  Expected Result: FAIL

──────────────────────────────
6. Test Case: FICO at Maximum Boundary with N_INQ at Lower Boundary
  • FICO = 900     // Valid FICO boundary value
  • N_INQ = 0     // Lowest typical value that satisfies N_INQ < 2
  Expected Result: PASS

──────────────────────────────
7. Test Case: FICO Below Lower Boundary with Valid N_INQ
  • FICO = 749     // Below the acceptable FICO threshold (>750)
  • N_INQ = 1     // Valid N_INQ but FICO condition fails
  Expected Result: FAIL

──────────────────────────────
Summary:
• To pass, FICO must be between 751 and 900 (inclusive of 900) and N_INQ must be less than 2.
• Values on or below 750 for FICO, above 900 for FICO, or 2 and above for N_INQ should cause the condition to fail.

These cases cover the edge boundaries for both FICO and N_INQ, ensuring that the condition is thoroughly tested at its limits.

Title: Proposal for a Dynamic GenAI Chatbot Solution

─────────────────────────────
1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
─────────────────────────────
In today’s rapidly evolving digital landscape, corporate clients demand chat solutions that grant flexibility, contextual adaptability, and continuous learning. Our Dynamic GenAI Chatbot offers an agile alternative to outdated, hardcoded chatbots. Leveraging next-generation AI, our solution transforms customer interactions by providing personalized, responsive, and context-driven conversations. This proposal outlines the strategic benefits, technological innovation, and implementation roadmap that make our GenAI solution the optimal choice for enterprise communications.

• Inconsistent or generic user interactions.

─────────────────────────────
4. BUSINESS VALUE & BENEFITS
─────────────────────────────

C. Competitive Advantage

instruction: What's the best way to implement Targeted Fast Gradient Sign Method in python?
output:
Below is one solid approach using PyTorch. The key idea in a targeted FGSM attack is to tweak the input in the direction that minimizes the loss for a specific (target) class. In contrast, the untargeted version increases the loss with respect to the true label. For a targeted attack you compute the gradient of the loss with respect to a desired target label and then subtract (rather than add) the sign of that gradient scaled by a small constant ε.

Below is an example implementation:

--------------------------------------------------
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def targeted_fgsm(model, x, target_label, epsilon):
    """
    Perform a targeted FGSM attack on input x so that the model predicts target_label.

    Arguments:
      model        -- the neural network model
      x            -- input tensor (e.g. an image), shape [N x C x H x W]
      target_label -- target label(s) (as torch.tensor) that we wish the model to misclassify x into
      epsilon      -- step size for the perturbation

    Returns:
      x_adv        -- adversarial example (torch tensor)
    """
    # Ensure the model is in evaluation mode and input is set to require gradients.
    model.eval()
    # Clone input and set requires_grad to True for gradient calculation.
    x_adv = x.clone().detach().to(x.device)
    x_adv.requires_grad = True

    # Forward pass. Use a suitable loss function such as cross-entropy.
    outputs = model(x_adv)
    
    # For a targeted attack, we want the network to predict target_label.
    # Hence, we minimize the loss with respect to the target label.
    loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(outputs, target_label)
    
    # Zero all existing gradients.
    model.zero_grad()
    
    # Backward pass to compute gradients of loss w.r.t. input x_adv.
    loss.backward()
    
    # Get the sign of the gradients.
    grad_sign = x_adv.grad.data.sign()
    
    # For targeted FGSM, we subtract the perturbation because we want to decrease the loss
    # for the target class (i.e. push the prediction toward the target).
    x_adv = x_adv - epsilon * grad_sign
    
    # Optionally, you might want to clip the adversarial example to ensure the pixel values are valid.
    x_adv = torch.clamp(x_adv, 0, 1)
    
    return x_adv

# Example usage:
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Assume we have a pretrained model and an input image x (of shape [1, C, H, W])
    # And we want to attack it so that the model predicts the target class 'target_label'.
    
    # Example dummy model
    class DummyModel(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
            super(DummyModel, self).__init__()
            self.fc = nn.Linear(28 * 28, num_classes)
        
        def forward(self, x):
            x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)  # Flatten, assuming input is like an MNIST image.
            return self.fc(x)
    
    # Create a dummy model and input.
    model = DummyModel(num_classes=10)
    x = torch.rand((1, 1, 28, 28))  # Random image
    target_label = torch.LongTensor([3])  # Suppose we want the model to output class 3
    epsilon = 0.1

    # Generate the adversarial example
    x_adv = targeted_fgsm(model, x, target_label, epsilon)
    
    # Check the predictions for the adversarial example.
    model.eval()
    pred = model(x_adv).max(1)[1]
    print("Adversarial prediction:", pred.item())
--------------------------------------------------

Explanation of the code:
1. We create a copy of the input and enable gradient tracking.
2. We perform a forward pass to compute the loss, using the target label in cross-entropy.
3. Calling backward() computes the gradients with respect to the input.
4. Instead of adding the sign of the gradient—as is done in an untargeted attack—we subtract it. This moves the sample in the direction that reduces the loss for the target label.
5. Finally, we clamp the resulting adversarial sample to maintain valid pixel ranges.

This implementation should work well for many standard networks. If you’re using another framework (for example, TensorFlow), the same general procedure applies:
• Compute gradients with respect to the input.
• Subtract a small perturbation in the direction of the sign of those gradients.
• Clip the perturbed image to valid ranges. 

This approach is considered “best” because it is simple, leverages automatic differentiation, and is easy to integrate into existing PyTorch workflows.

instruction: Explain in detail the concept of deep double descent in the context of training machine learning models. Describe how it is related to gradient descent and early stopping.
output:
Deep double descent is a phenomenon in modern machine learning that challenges the traditional bias–variance tradeoff picture. In classical statistics, one typically expects that as model capacity increases, the test error follows a U-shaped curve: it decreases initially (reducing bias) and then increases past a certain point (due to overfitting and high variance). However, research on deep neural networks and other modern models has shown that if you continue to increase model capacity (or training time), the test error can actually decrease again—thus creating a “double descent” curve with two downward slopes separated by a peak.

Below is a detailed explanation of the concept, its connection to gradient descent, and how early stopping comes into play:

1. What Is Deep Double Descent?

 a. Traditional U-shaped Curve:  
  • In classical learning theory, as model complexity grows, the error on unseen data typically first decreases—because the model can capture more structure—but after a certain point, the risk of overfitting causes test error to rise.  
  • The peak typically happens near the “interpolation threshold,” where the model just barely fits (or overfits) the training data exactly.

 b. The Double Descent Phenomenon:  
  • In many modern practice settings, especially with deep neural networks and highly overparameterized models, if you continue increasing model capacity—even beyond the point where the model interpolates the training data—the test error begins to decline again.  
  • This second descent suggests that heavily overparameterized models, when trained properly, can generalize better than models that are just barely complex enough to fit the data.
  • The overall error vs. model capacity curve hence shows an initial descent (underfitting to a good fit), a peak (overfitting at the interpolation threshold), and then a second descent (improved generalization due to implicit regularization among other factors).

2. The Mechanisms Behind Deep Double Descent

 a. The Role of Overparameterization:  
  • When a model has more parameters than training examples—or more capacity than needed—the optimization process (usually through gradient descent) can find solutions that interpolate the data while still being “simple” in other senses (e.g., having low norm or residing in a “good” region of the parameter space).  
  • Such multiple solutions exist, and gradient-based methods have an implicit bias (or implicit regularization) that tends to select “simpler” solutions that generalize well.

 b. The Role of Gradient Descent:  
  • Gradient descent (and its variants) is the standard optimization method for training deep neural networks. Its step-by-step update rule does not simply minimize the training loss but also plays a role in which solution is eventually found.  
  • Even when many parameter configurations yield zero training error (i.e., they interpolate the data), the trajectory taken by gradient descent often converges to solutions with favorable properties, such as lower complexity in a certain sense (for instance, smaller norm in linear models).  
  • This implicit regularization of gradient descent can, therefore, explain why a model in the overparameterized regime—despite being capable of fitting arbitrary labels—ends up generalizing well after sufficient training. This is one of the factors behind the second descent phase in the double descent curve.

3. Early Stopping and Its Connection

 a. Early Stopping as Regularization:  
  • Early stopping is a practical regularization technique where one stops training before the model fully minimizes the training loss.  
  • In high-capacity models, if overfitting is a risk, early stopping can prevent the optimizer from converging to an overfitted solution.
  • Early stopping leverages the dynamic trajectory of gradient descent; during the early epochs, the model is picking up the dominant and robust patterns in the data, whereas prolonged training may allow the model to start fitting noise.

 b. How Early Stopping Relates to Double Descent:  
  • In the context of double descent, one can also observe a “epoch-wise” double descent phenomenon where, as training progresses, the test error initially decreases, then sometimes temporarily increases, and might decrease again if training is continued further.  
  • Early stopping, therefore, lets practitioners choose a point in training where the model has captured the essential patterns without starting to overfit on noise.
  • In some cases, if the model is sufficiently overparameterized, training longer might eventually bring the test error down again (the second descent). However, if computational resources or stability concerns are paramount, early stopping is still used as a safeguard against the worst overfitting behavior around the interpolation threshold before the second descent is observed.
  • Essentially, early stopping interacts with double descent in that it is a way to “pick” a favorable point on the training curve where the undesired increase in test error is avoided—even though, paradoxically, longer training in an overparameterized regime might ultimately lead to better performance through the mechanisms of implicit regularization.

4. Insights and Practical Takeaways

 • Understanding double descent can inform decisions on model design. It suggests that increasing model capacity beyond what was traditionally considered safe can actually improve generalization, provided that the optimization (using gradient descent) is managed correctly.
 • The phenomenon highlights the importance of the training dynamics. The path taken by gradient descent through parameter space matters as much as the final optimization objective.
 • Early stopping becomes one tool among many to harness these dynamics effectively, thereby ensuring that training halts before the model starts fitting noise, or equivalently, when the model is at a favorable part of the double descent curve.
 • Researchers and practitioners now monitor not only model capacity but also training schedule and learning dynamics to understand where their models lie on the double descent spectrum.

In summary, deep double descent reveals that in many modern, highly overparameterized models, increasing capacity can lead to a counterintuitive second improvement in test performance—as a result of the interplay between model structure, the implicit regularization provided by gradient descent, and training dynamics. Early stopping is one method to leverage the beneficial phases of training while avoiding the pitfalls of premature overfitting, thus helping practitioners navigate the double descent landscape effectively.

def analyze_code(input_code):             
	# Format code into strings and sentences for NLP     
	code_str = " ".join(input_code.split())        
	sentences = [s.strip() for s in code_str.split(".") if s.strip()]   
	#Extract relevant info and intent from code        
	variables = []              
	functions = []    
	logic = []       
	for sentence in sentences: 
		if "=" in sentence:           
			variables.append(sentence.split("=")[0].strip())       
		elif "(" in sentence:            
			functions.append(sentence.split("(")[0].strip())       
		else:           
			logic.append(sentence)               
	#Return info and intent in dictionary    
	return {"variables": variables, "functions": functions, "logic": logic}

# Define function to generate prompt from analyzed code  
def generate_prompt(code_analysis):       
	prompt = f"Generate code with the following: \n\n"

	prompt += f"Functions: {', '.join(code_analysis['functions'])} \n\n"   
	prompt += f"Logic: {' '.join(code_analysis['logic'])}"  
	return prompt

instruction: Visualize pandas dataframe in gradio
output:
Below is an example of how you can visualize a pandas DataFrame using Gradio. Gradio provides a DataFrame component that lets you display—and even interact with—a DataFrame in your web interface.

Below is a complete example:

-------------------------------------------------
# Sample Code

import gradio as gr
import pandas as pd

# Create a sample pandas DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 35],
    "Country": ["USA", "Canada", "UK"]
})

# This function simply returns the DataFrame
def get_dataframe():
    return df

# Create a Gradio interface that outputs a DataFrame.
# Here we use gr.DataFrame as the output component.
demo = gr.Interface(
    fn=get_dataframe,                # function to be called
    inputs=[],                       # no inputs; just display the DataFrame from the function
    outputs=gr.DataFrame(label="My DataFrame")  # display the DataFrame with a label
)

# Launch the Gradio app
demo.launch()

-------------------------------------------------

Explanation:

1. We first import the necessary libraries: pandas for data manipulation and gradio for creating the UI.
2. We create a pandas DataFrame with sample data.
3. The function get_dataframe is defined to simply return the DataFrame.
4. We configure the Gradio interface (using gr.Interface) with:
   • No inputs (since we’re only visualizing static data).
   • An output that uses gr.DataFrame to render the DataFrame on the web interface.
5. Finally, demo.launch() starts the Gradio application.

When you run this script, it will start a local Gradio app in your browser that displays the DataFrame. You can expand this example by adding interactivity (like allowing the user to modify the data or input parameters) if required.

instruction: Can you explain to me how to forecast revenue for an online business vs. a brick and mortar retailer?  What are the key differences?
output:
Forecasting revenue for an online business versus a brick‐and‐mortar retailer involves many of the same fundamental forecasting principles—examining historical data, seasonality, market trends, and strategic initiatives—but the specifics of the data, variables, and assumptions can differ significantly between the two. Below are some key factors and differences to consider:

1. Data Sources and Metrics

• Online Business:
 – Traffic & Engagement: Web analytics (e.g., site visits, page views, bounce rates, session duration) are primary drivers. Forecasts often rely on trends in digital traffic and conversion rates.
 – Conversion Funnels: Detailed online funnel data (e.g., click-through rates, cart abandonment rates) help predict sales based on customer behavior.
 – Digital Marketing Channels: Revenue is heavily influenced by online marketing (SEO, SEM, email campaigns, social media), so measuring the performance of each channel is crucial.
 – Global Reach: Online businesses typically serve a national or global customer base, meaning revenue can be impacted by broader trends in e-commerce, international market growth, or changes in digital regulations.

• Brick‐and‐Mortar Retailer:
 – Foot Traffic: The number of visitors or customers physically entering the store is a key metric; historical footfall data and its fluctuations (perhaps influenced by weather, local events, or day of the week) are closely tracked.
 – In-Store Conversion: Sales figures are often tied directly to how many visitors convert into buyers. Local customer behaviors, loyalty trends, and in-store promotions affect conversion.
 – Local Demographics: Revenue forecasting must consider the demographics, local economic conditions, or a competitor’s presence close to the store.
 – Operational Constraints: Physical inventory, staffing, and store capacity can limit sales, factors that generally are less restrictive in the online world.

2. Seasonality and External Influences

• Online Business:
 – Often experiences rapid fluctuations based on digital trends, viral marketing impacts, or even online sales events (like Cyber Monday). 
 – Can react quickly to changes in search engine algorithms or social media trends that might affect traffic and revenue.
 – Global events (e.g., international holidays, global pandemics) can have immediate effects on online consumer behavior, though the delay may be shorter or more nuanced than in physical retail.

• Brick‐and‐Mortar Retailer:
 – Local seasonality, such as holiday shopping weather or regional events, often drives predictable cycles in foot traffic.
 – Changes in local economic conditions (like a new competitor opening or a major employer leaving the area) can alter revenue trends.
 – In-store promotions, community events, and local advertising play a more pronounced role in revenue generation than in the online space.

3. Operational and Marketing Flexibility

• Online Business:
 – Often enjoys greater flexibility in adjusting pricing, launching promotions, or experimenting with marketing strategies in real time. These adjustments can be quickly tracked and iterated.
 – Forecasting models tend to include agile metrics such as real-time conversion tracking, A/B testing impacts, and rapid market feedback loops.

• Brick‐and‐Mortar Retailer:
 – May have slower reaction times due to logistics, physical layout changes, and longer-term supplier or staffing contracts.
 – Forecasting frequently includes planning for lead times in merchandising changes, store renovations, or staffing adjustments which have been planned well in advance.

4. Impact of Technology and Automation

• Online Business:
 – Leverages automated analytics, real-time dashboards, and advanced attribution models that help correlate online behavior to revenue changes almost immediately.
 – Can test scenarios quickly with robust digital data, allowing revenue models to be fine-tuned in near real time.

• Brick‐and‐Mortar Retailer:
 – Might rely more on historical data and periodic surveys of customer sentiment, since the physical experience isn’t captured as dynamically.
 – While technology (such as Wi-Fi tracking or point-of-sale data) can provide insights, adjustments often take longer to implement due to the inherent physical constraints.

5. Forecasting Methods

Both models may employ:
 – Time-Series Forecasting: Using historical sales data, trend analysis, and seasonal adjustments.
 – Scenario-Based Forecasting: Considering various “what-if” scenarios like marketing spend increases, changes in local competition (for brick and mortar), or shifts in digital ad performance (for online).
 – Regression or Machine Learning Models: Tying variables (e.g., digital ad spend, website traffic, local economic indicators) to revenue patterns.

For an online business, the model may emphasize leading indicators (traffic, click-throughs) that immediately translate into revenue, whereas for a brick‐and‐mortar retailer, models may lean more on lagging indicators (historical foot traffic, in-store sales trends) combined with external local data.

In summary, while both types of businesses need to account for historical performance, market trends, and operational strategies in their revenue forecasts, the key differences lie in the specific metrics tracked, the speed of feedback and adjustments, and the contextual factors (global digital vs. local physical market dynamics) that drive sales. Tailoring the forecasting process to these factors will result in more accurate projections and better strategic decisions.

Below is an example cocotb testbench for a multiplier. In this example, we assume that your multiplier DUT has two inputs named “a” and “b” and an output named “out.” If your DUT uses a clock (for example in a pipelined design), you may have a clock input “clk” that you need to drive. You can adjust the names and timing as needed for your specific design.

Save the following code (for example as multiplier_tb.py) in your simulation directory:

------------------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
A simple cocotb testbench for a multiplier.
This example assumes the multiplier has two inputs:
   a, b
and one output:
   out
If your design is sequential and uses a clock, this testbench will start
a clock on dut.clk. Otherwise, you can remove the clock-generation code.
"""

import cocotb
from cocotb.clock import Clock
from cocotb.triggers import RisingEdge, Timer
import random

@cocotb.test()
async def multiplier_test(dut):
    """
    Test the multiplier with a few predefined and random values.
    """

    # If your DUT requires a clock, start it (assumed period = 10 ns)
    if hasattr(dut, "clk"):
        clock = Clock(dut.clk, 10, units="ns")
        cocotb.start_soon(clock.start())
        # Wait a short time for the clock to stabilize
        await Timer(20, units="ns")
        dut._log.info("Clock started")

    # List of test vectors (a, b)
    test_vectors = [
        (0, 0),
        (1, 1),
        (2, 3),
        (15, 15),
        (255, 255),
        (17, 23)
    ]

    # Test each pre-defined test vector
    for a_val, b_val in test_vectors:
        dut.a.value = a_val
        dut.b.value = b_val
        dut._log.info(f"Applying stimulus: a={a_val}, b={b_val}")
        
        # If the design is combinational, a short delay may be enough.
        # If sequential, you may need to wait for a clock edge or multiple cycles.
        await Timer(10, units="ns")

        expected = a_val * b_val
        actual = int(dut.out.value)

        assert actual == expected, (
            f"Test failed for a={a_val}, b={b_val}: expected {expected}, got {actual}"
        )
        dut._log.info(f"Test passed for a={a_val}, b={b_val}: {expected} == {actual}")

    # Optionally, some random tests
    NUM_RANDOM_TESTS = 10
    for _ in range(NUM_RANDOM_TESTS):
        a_val = random.randint(0, 255)
        b_val = random.randint(0, 255)
        dut.a.value = a_val
        dut.b.value = b_val
        dut._log.info(f"Applying random stimulus: a={a_val}, b={b_val}")
        
        await Timer(10, units="ns")
        expected = a_val * b_val
        actual = int(dut.out.value)
        assert actual == expected, (
            f"Random test failed for a={a_val}, b={b_val}: expected {expected}, got {actual}"
        )
        dut._log.info(f"Random test passed for a={a_val}, b={b_val}")

    dut._log.info("All multiplier tests passed successfully.")
------------------------------------------------------------

Notes:
1. Adjust the port names (a, b, out, clk) if your DUT uses different names.
2. If your multiplier is synchronous, you might want to use RisingEdge(dut.clk) instead of Timer delays.
3. To run the testbench, make sure you have cocotb installed and that your simulator is configured properly. For example:
  make SIM=<your_simulator>
4. If you want to add more tests or vary the delay, feel free to modify the code.

This testbench applies several static and random test cases to verify that the multiplier produces the correct result.

Below is one option for a low‐carb breakfast that’s both satisfying and nutrient dense:

Low‐Carb Spinach, Mushroom, and Avocado Omelette

Ingredients:
• 2 large eggs  
• A generous handful (≈1 cup) fresh spinach  
• ½ cup sliced mushrooms  
• 1 ounce (about 1/4 cup) crumbled feta or shredded cheddar (optional)  
• ½ of a medium avocado, sliced  
• Salt and pepper to taste  
• A small drizzle of olive oil or a pat of butter for cooking

Preparation:
1. Heat a nonstick skillet over medium heat and add a bit of olive oil or butter.  
2. Sauté the mushrooms for about 2 minutes until they start softening, then add the spinach and cook until just wilted (about 1 minute).  
3. While the vegetables are cooking, beat the eggs in a bowl with a little salt and pepper.  
4. Pour the eggs into the pan with the veggies. Let the eggs set for a moment, then sprinkle the crumbled cheese evenly over the top (if using).  
5. Once the omelette starts to firm up, gently fold it in half. Continue cooking until the eggs are fully set.  
6. Plate your omelette and serve with the sliced avocado on the side.

Estimated Carbohydrates Breakdown (approximate values):
• 2 large eggs – about 1–1.5 grams of carbs (eggs are very low in carbs)  
• 1 cup spinach – roughly 0.4 grams of carbs  
• ½ cup mushrooms – about 1 gram of carbs  
• 1 ounce cheese – around 0.5–1 gram of carbs (varies by type)  
• ½ medium avocado – approximately 6–7 grams total carbs; however, much of this is fiber. Most low-carb counts focus on “net carbs.” A half avocado typically offers about 2–3 grams of net carbs.

Total estimated net carbohydrates: roughly 5–7 grams

This breakfast delivers a good mix of protein, healthy fats, and fiber while keeping the carbohydrate content very low—perfect if you’re keeping an eye on your carb intake. Enjoy!

instruction: Provide me with a breakfast recipe that is quick to make and is high in protien (at least 30 grams) and has a variety of ingredients
output:
Try this Protein-Packed Veggie Breakfast Wrap that combines eggs, lean turkey sausage, fiber-rich vegetables, and a whole-grain wrap. It’s designed to be ready in about 10 minutes and packs over 30 grams of protein.

Ingredients (serves 1):
• 2 whole eggs (≈12 g protein)  
• 2 egg whites (≈8 g protein)  
• 1 small turkey sausage (or 2 turkey links) – roughly 8–10 g protein  
• ¼ cup black beans (optional, adds extra protein and fiber)  
• 1 cup fresh spinach leaves  
• ½ red bell pepper, diced  
• ¼ cup cherry tomatoes, halved  
• 2 tablespoons shredded low-fat cheddar or mozzarella cheese (optional)  
• 1 whole-wheat tortilla (or high-protein wrap)  
• Salt and pepper, to taste  
• 1 teaspoon olive oil  
• Salsa or hot sauce for serving (optional)  

Instructions:
1. Prep the Veggies: Rinse the spinach and tomatoes. Dice the red bell pepper and halve the cherry tomatoes. Drain and rinse the black beans if you’re using them.

2. Whisk Eggs: In a medium bowl, crack the 2 eggs and add the 2 egg whites. Whisk until well combined. Season lightly with salt and pepper.

3. Cook Turkey Sausage: Slice your turkey sausage into bite-sized pieces. Heat the olive oil in a nonstick skillet over medium-high heat, and sauté the sausage slices for about 1–2 minutes until they start to brown. (If using pre-cooked sausage links, simply warm them.)

4. Sauté Veggies: Add the diced red bell pepper and spinach to the skillet. Sauté for about 1 minute so that the spinach wilts slightly. Then, add the cherry tomatoes and black beans, stirring briefly so everything heats through but remains slightly crisp.

5. Make the Omelette: Pour the egg mixture over the veggies and sausage, swirling the pan so that the eggs envelop the ingredients. Allow the eggs to set for about 1–2 minutes. Optionally, sprinkle the shredded cheese over the top. Gently scramble or let it cook as an omelette until the eggs are fully set (about 2–3 minutes total).

6. Assemble the Wrap: Warm the whole-wheat tortilla in a dry skillet or microwave for 10–15 seconds to make it flexible. Spoon the egg and veggie scramble onto the center of the tortilla. Add a dollop of salsa or hot sauce if desired.

7. Roll and Serve: Fold the bottom up over the filling, then the sides in, and roll tightly. Enjoy your protein-packed, veggie-loaded breakfast wrap immediately!

Nutrition Note: This meal provides a balance of lean protein (from eggs, egg whites, and turkey sausage), fiber and vitamins from the vegetables, and whole grains from the tortilla. Depending on the exact sausage and wrap brands used, you should comfortably get at least 30 grams of protein.

Feel free to customize the vegetables or substitute with others you enjoy. This quick breakfast is perfect for busy mornings while still offering a variety of flavors and nutrients. Enjoy!

How are our historic stone houses built and what problems do stone structures face today?
I have been trying to read up on natural stone masonry, and in particular trying to find examples of constructions where both natural stone and brick have been used in the same construction. The overwhelming majority of our historic buildings are in stone, and not infrequently they have, if not entire walls of natural stone, then at least elements of natural stone.
The focus of this compilation has been to read about a wide range of topics in the field of natural stone masonry, but perhaps the most focus has been on craft processes and descriptions of approaches to the material.
Which stone is used where varies greatly from place to place, so the magnifying glass has also ended up reading about the difference in materials across the country, as well as the problems we face in the conservation and restoration of natural stone structures today.
Natural stone is a material that has historically been used in Sweden since before the advent of bricks. Our early stone buildings were built by cold masonry where stones were stacked on top of each other without the use of mortar or other binders.
However, natural stone has had difficulty asserting itself in buildings outside of high-rise buildings such as churches, manor houses and mansions, partly because of the ingrained tradition of building residential buildings in wood, but also because it was an expensive material, both in terms of transportation if the material was not close at hand, but also in terms of processing.
In 1766, at a time when there was a shortage of wood for building houses, and even a promise of a 20-year tax exemption if you built your house in stone, Carl Wijnblad writes about how natural stone was difficult to handle and unsuitable for building houses. Here, however, he is talking about natural stone in the form of gray stone, a collective term for blocks of stone picked directly from the ground or dug up, for example, during agricultural work, and not about the brick, which he warmly advocated in his book Beskrifning, huru allmogens buildings, so of stone, as well as trees, must be erected with the greatest economy, according to attached project drawings in six copper pieces, as well as proposals for necessary building materials. He found the stone unsuitable as it requires a lot of processing and a lot of lime to be good enough to be used other than for foundation walls and cellars. The stone was also considered to be damp and cold, and suitable only for animal houses.
Buildings made of both natural stone, in the form of grey stone, and brick in the same construction are described in a number of different designs in the training material from Hermods in the document Byggnadskonstruktionslära (för murare) : undervisning per korrespondens (1907). In the chapter Walls of stone blocks: "Such walls of stone blocks, which are to have any appreciable height, are, however, erected as mixed walls, i.e. they are erected with horizontal bands and vertical columns of brick". This also clarifies several other
approaches to the inclusion of bricks in natural stone walls, with bricks or more tumbled stones being used in virtually all parts of the wall where greater precision is required. Window surrounds, the corners of the wall, the above-mentioned stabilizing shifts, and even roof ends should be made of brick. Hermod's text is relatively exhaustive in the field of natural stone masonry, and describes various approaches to stones in differently worked conditions, but no information about who or where these experiences and approaches come from is given in the text. The text is familiarly signed by Hermods himself, but it is doubtful that he is the author.
Further reading in, for example, Arvid Henström's book Landtbyggnadskonsten volume 5 (1869) offers a slightly more detailed account of the building method, but in general the advice sounds the same as in Hermod's text. As an engineer, Henström should be well versed in the art of building, and his recommendations are sound, even if the text itself is not significantly exhaustive in terms of illustrations or other aids other than a running text description of different approaches to masonry with natural stone.
The fact that someone like Henström is giving the same advice as Hermods gives good credit to the fact that the information in the training material is sound and well based on literature in the field.
However, Henström makes it clear already in the introduction to this text that it is not written for the experienced craftsman, but "it is intended for the farmer and his inexperienced workers who are unfamiliar with building details and their form and execution", which explains the lack of drawing examples and more detailed descriptions of the craft processes. Both texts recommend the use of the best quality hydraulic lime mortar for masonry.
One conclusion to be drawn from reading both Hermod's and Henström's texts is that the construction of a stone wall does not differ so dramatically, whether it is built of brick or natural stone. The goal is to achieve a joint where the different building blocks interact with each other to create a stable structure that can withstand forces from different directions, but different solutions need to be applied depending on how processed the stones are. Both provide insight into the role that brick can play in natural stone construction, and are described as the rational choice in many cases. Neither text is exhaustive, or should be seen as detailed descriptions of craft processes, but they can be used, with a little prior knowledge, as a complement to the execution of masonry with natural stone.
Structures using relatively unprocessed natural stone face a number of problems in addition to those encountered during construction.
The Geological Society London publishes a journal that compiles information and articles in the field. The journal itself is locked behind fees, but the introduction was available for guidance to other authors in the field. The introduction is written by Professor of Geology Siegesmund Siegfried, who in his text highlights the problems faced in the preservation and restoration of natural stone buildings. Strategies on how to deal with damage caused by natural degradation of the stone, how the environment influences the grading, how anthropogenic circumstances accelerate decay, attack by algae or microorganisms in the stone.
The reading of Siegesmund's text therefore led me on a trail of other texts in the field, and eventually to the article Impact of the surface roughness of stones used in historical buildings on biodeterioration, a text on how the surface texture porosity of building stones influences the speed and degree of biological impact and degradation.

Biological impact refers to plants, both clinging plants with roots and creeping plants such as lichens and mosses, and their impact on the structure of the stone, both as living and dead material. The material is based on investigations carried out in Nigde, Turkey, which is somewhat different from conditions in Sweden, but the different types of rocks investigated are similar to those used in Sweden, such as large amounts of limestone. The source is really only tangentially relevant to this compilation, but interesting reading nonetheless, and definitely a recurring topic in the question of how our stone houses should be taken care of.
Sources
● Henström, Arvid (1869) Practical handbook in the art of rural construction: including the study of building materials, the processing and joining of building materials, the shape, dimensions and strength of building components .... Örebro: Beijer
● Hermods (1907) Teaching and correspondence, Building construction for bricklayers, seventh letter.
● Mustafa Korkanç, Ahmet Savran (2015) Impact of the surface roughness of stones used in historical buildings on biodeterioration.
● Wijnbladh, Carl (1766). Description of how the common people's buildings, both of stone and wood, may be erected with the greatest economy, according to attached

project drawings in six copper pieces, and proposals for necessary building materials. Utgifwen på kongl. maj:ts allernådigste befehlung, efter föregångit gillande wid riks-dagen år 1765, af Carl Wijnblad. Stockholm, printed by Peter Heszelberg, 1766. Stockholm: (Hesselberg!

1. Describing the Content of the Sources

 a. Overview and Depth:  
  • While the summary provides a lot of factual detail from each source, it could benefit from a clearer “overview” section at the beginning. This should briefly outline the scope, focus, and historical context of each source before delving into specifics.

 a. Assessing Authority and Context:  
  • Although the text refers to some historical credibility (e.g., the recommendation by Henström and the critique about Hermods’ credentials), it would be useful to more explicitly evaluate each source. For example, discuss how the age of the texts (Wijnblad, Hermods, Henström) might affect their reliability in the current context of conservation studies.

 b. Strengths and Weaknesses:

  • Showing how these strengths and weaknesses inform the overall understanding of the historical and practical aspects of stone masonry would further enhance the critical evaluation.

 c. Methodological Critique:
